title: Popular Film and Television Comedy
finding: Book surveying the diversity of screen comedy forms (feature narratives, sketches and shorts, sitcom and variety, slapstick, romance) and relating them to comedy's basic conventions (happy endings, gags, humour and laughter) and their institutional contexts (per authors). Theoretical/historical overview, no empirical data.
why_for_us: Useful vocabulary for deciding whether each Komputerku episode is a gag-led sketch or a narrative micro-episode with a mini-resolution; the series needs both a gag and a small story turn.

title: Understanding the Sitcom
finding: Book chapter describing sitcom narrative and stylistic conventions; argues that the two essential attributes of broadcast-era sitcom storytelling are a repeatable premise and episodes segmented to allow commercial interruptions (per author).
why_for_us: A repeatable premise (notary office + 'feed the little computer' problem) is the core asset; each 60-90 s episode is effectively one segment between 'breaks' (the next swipe), so it needs its own button ending.

title: Comedy Verité? The Observational Documentary Meets the Televisual Sitcom
finding: Essay arguing that 'comedy verité' (handheld camera, awkward pacing, continuity violations borrowed from observational documentary, as in Arrested Development and The Office) is best understood as an emerging mode of production adopted for efficiency, visual complexity and semiotic clout, rather than a subgenre (per author).
why_for_us: A pseudo-documentary look (static 'office camera', occasional glance to lens) is cheap, forgiving of imperfect AI video and fits short vertical clips; it can be the series' default visual grammar.

title: Participation frameworks and participation in televised sitcom, candid camera and stand-up comedy
finding: Pragmatic analysis reconstructing participation frameworks of sitcom, candid camera and stand-up: the viewer is the ratified recipient of the production team's discourse while camera position, sound and other technical means create a fictitious overhearer position at the level of the characters (per author). Theoretical, no audience data.
why_for_us: Decide per scene whether the viewer is an overhearer (classic sitcom framing) or directly addressed (look to camera); mixing both deliberately is a known meta-humour tool.

title: Through the Gaps of My Fingers: Genre, Femininity, and Cringe Aesthetics in Dramedy Television
finding: Textual analysis of Girls, Fleabag and Insecure: cringe aesthetics in female-centred prestige dramedy negotiate tensions between drama and comedy, and character 'complexity' shifts the comedy toward the more prestigious dramatic mode (per authors). Essay, no audience data.
why_for_us: Cringe in dramedy works through character complexity; Kuba's literal-mindedness should cause embarrassment that reveals character, not only slapstick.

title: The Cringe and the Sneer: Structures of Feeling in Veep
finding: Essay arguing that no cringe comedy makes viewers cringe for its whole duration: such comedies alternate tipping points where schadenfreude tips into cringe and back, constantly recalibrating viewer-character distance; Veep interlaces cringe with a 'sneer' affect (per author). Case study, MDPI venue.
why_for_us: Ration cringe: one awkward peak per 60-90 s episode, then release, rather than sustained embarrassment that viewers may swipe away from.

title: A humor typology to identify humor styles used in sitcoms
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Developed a sitcom-specific typology of humour techniques, tested for inter-coder reliability, and applied it to four well-known US sitcoms; the techniques used aligned with superiority and incongruity theories (per authors). Content analysis; no audience outcome in this paper.
why_for_us: A reliable coding scheme the team can use to audit scripts: tag every joke by technique to check variety across the season instead of repeating one device.

title: More than Just a Laughing Matter: A Coding Framework of Humor in Media Entertainment for Tweens and Teens
finding: Content analysis of 107 TV series (5,633 scenes) named as favourites by 10-14-year-olds confirmed ten humour types; aggressive humour was present in 87.9% of series and coping humour in only 23.4%, and types frequently co-occurred (per authors).
why_for_us: Popular series lean on aggressive humour; a gentler office comedy can stand out with coping and self-defeating humour (Helena's dryness, Kuba's mishaps), but expect to mix types within a scene.

title: Episoden des Alltäglichen - Sitcoms und Gesellschaft: Eine wissenssoziologische und hermeneutische Lektüre
finding: German sociology-of-knowledge book arguing that, unlike series that look beyond viewers' lifeworld, the sitcom has for over half a century focused on everyday themes within viewers' horizon and delivers pointed descriptions of everyday life (per author).
why_for_us: The notary office is an everyday institution most Poles know; anchor gags in recognisable daily routines (queues, signatures, stamps) rather than exotic legal scenarios.

title: A processing fluency-account of funniness: Running gags and spoiling punchlines
finding: Four experiments: pre-exposing key punchline words 15 min or even 1 min before a joke increased its funniness ratings, whereas pre-exposure directly before the joke decreased them; pre-exposing the joke's beginning had no effect, and a font-fluency manipulation replicated the effect (per authors). The authors interpret this as a processing-fluency mechanism behind running gags.
why_for_us: The 'did anyone feed the little computer?' gag should be planted early and recur after a gap (not twice in a row within seconds); its payoff line can reuse words the viewer already heard in earlier episodes.

title: Catchphrases: a semiotic, genealogical and cultural materialist study of the form
finding: Essay arguing that catchphrases work like proverbs in oral cultures: a mutually recognisable cultural shorthand for larger ideas, characters and stereotypes, embodying 'a form of knowing that revels in the already known', which may explain their 'lowbrow' reputation among intellectual audiences (per author).
why_for_us: 'Did anyone feed the little computer?' should become shorthand for the whole AI-cost theme; its pleasure is recognition, so keep the wording fixed and vary only who says it and when.

title: Eternal Recurrence: Not Again!
finding: Philosophy chapter observing that repetition alone can suffice for comedy (a plank falling every time it is repositioned, Monty Python returning to 'the larch'), with laughter arising from sheer redundancy (per author).
why_for_us: Supports making the running gag funnier by sheer persistence, provided it is visibly the same each time.

title: A Multivariate Study of the Effect of Repetition on Humor Appreciation as Qualified by two Social Influence Factors
finding: 64 undergraduates rated 25 audio 'bloopers' twice, alone or in groups of 12-17, with or without recorded laughter: decreases with repetition were more common in group than individual settings and affected smiling most; alone, only smile ratings fell and only when the second presentation lacked recorded laughter (per authors). Exact repetition of the same material, small sample.
why_for_us: Verbatim re-showing of the same joke wears out; the running gag must recur as the same line in a new situation, not as a replayed clip.

title: Le Ragotin de Scarron ou la vitalité du comique de répétition
finding: Literary essay: the character Ragotin in Scarron's Roman comique combines all of Bergson's types of comique de répétition (the jack-in-the-box, the puppet, the snowball effect), and his mechanisation serves to expose rigid behaviour (per author).
why_for_us: Bergson's 'snowball' gives the escalation model for the season: each recurrence of 'feed the little computer' should raise the stakes slightly until Helena's finale line.

title: Timing in the performance of jokes
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Acoustic analysis of 20 joke performances found no significant change in speech rate at or around the punchline and no evidence that punchlines are preceded by pauses; no differences between prepared and spontaneous jokes (per authors). Small sample; the authors conclude timing theory needs more research.
why_for_us: Do not rely on a long synthetic pause before every punchline as the 'timing trick' for AI voices; test pause length empirically per line instead of applying a fixed rule.

title: Prosodic Markers of Saliency in Humorous Narratives
finding: Instrumental measurement of pitch, volume and speech rate in told jokes showed punchlines were not louder, but delivered at significantly lower pitch and slower speech rate than the preceding text, often with laughing or smiling voice, and were not preceded by significant pauses (per authors); they attribute this to the punchline's final position rather than its saliency.
why_for_us: For Helena's dry punchlines, direct the TTS toward a lower pitch and slightly slower delivery on the final line rather than louder emphasis or an extra pause.

title: Prosodic Markers in Mandarin Stand-Up Comedy: An Acoustic and Perceptual Study of Pauses
finding: Corpus of about 80 min of professional Mandarin stand-up: pre-punchline pauses were on average 157 ms longer than the speaker's baseline pauses; but in a perception study with resynthesised jokes at five pre-punchline pause durations, funniness ratings did not differ (per authors). Production-perception mismatch; conference paper, audio-only, unfamiliar jokes.
why_for_us: A slightly lengthened pause before the punchline is what performers do, but content carries most of the laugh; spend effort on the line itself and use the pause as a light cue, not a fix.

title: Prosodic Analysis of Humor in Stand-up Comedy
venue: Journal of English Language Literature and Education
finding: Praat analysis of Trevor Noah's stand-up (pitch, volume, pause) reported that the comedian used a substantial pause before punchlines, which the authors claim created humour (per authors). Single performer, no listener test, small regional journal.
why_for_us: Shows only that a well-known comedian pauses before punchlines; contrasts with Pickering et al. and is not evidence that pauses cause laughs.

title: Prosody of humor in Sex and the City
finding: Exploratory study of conversational humour in the HBO series: pitch variation and pauses form part of a prosodic bundle that both marks and helps create humorous utterances (per authors). Exploratory, scripted TV dialogue, no audience measures.
why_for_us: Scripted screen dialogue does use pitch and pauses as humour markers, so voice direction (not just text) belongs in each episode's script notes for the AI voices.

title: Prosodic and multimodal markers of humor in conversation
finding: Case study of conversational humour: humour was not marked by higher pitch or volume, faster speech or significant pauses, but smiling and laughter tended to co-occur with humour (per authors). Case study, conversation not performance.
why_for_us: In natural-sounding banter the cue that something is a joke is the smile in the voice or face, not loudness; for avatars with weak faces, a smiling-voice setting on Marta or Basia can do that signalling.

title: Comic Timing in Contemporary Slapstick Films
finding: Theoretical essay defining comic timing as perceived durational incongruity: in the standard form the gag setup lasts longer than the payoff, while in a non-standard form extended duration becomes self-referential and subverts the spectator's expectations (per author). No empirical test.
why_for_us: In a 60-90 s episode keep the setup longer than a very short payoff, and reserve the deliberately over-long beat (an awkward hold on Kuba) as a rare variation.

title: Cryptic Emotions and the Emergence of a Metatheory of Mind in Popular Filmmaking
finding: In a sample of Hollywood films 1940-2010 the prevalence of 'cryptic' reaction shots (an unspeaking character with modest, slightly negative and slightly aroused facial expression) grew dramatically; they tend to come at the end of conversations and scenes and leave viewers speculating about the character's thoughts (per authors). Corpus analysis, not comedy-specific.
why_for_us: A short silent reaction shot with a minimal expression is a standard, well-tolerated device, which suits avatars with limited facial range: end scenes on Helena's near-neutral look instead of an exaggerated grimace.

title: Does the Kuleshov Effect Really Exist? Revisiting a Classic Film Experiment on Facial Expressions and Emotional Contexts
finding: Behavioural and eye-tracking replication with 36 participants and 24 sequences of neutral faces across six emotional contexts: participants chose the context-congruent emotion category more often than alternatives and valence/arousal ratings moved in the expected direction, though eye-tracking did not differ by condition (per authors).
why_for_us: Editing a neutral avatar face against a telling insert (an empty credit meter, a client's document) makes viewers read emotion into it; cutting can compensate for limited facial expressivity.

title: Waves of laughter: comic surfing on Bergson’s mechanical inelasticity
finding: Essay arguing that Bergson's 'mechanical inelasticity' is too inhuman to have much practical value for comic performers, and that his emphasis on human flexibility and laughter as a social 'wave' matters more for performance (per authors).
why_for_us: Don't make Kuba a pure literal-minded machine; his rigidity is funny only if the human behind it shows, and the joke lands best when the others' reactions ripple around it.

title: Why is the straight 'man' in animation usually a woman?
finding: Practitioner conference paper: the author's half-animated comedy pilot had no 'straight' character and felt 'too loud', leaving no space to frame gags; she argues scripted comedy needs a straight role and 'down time', and observes that in animated sitcoms the straight role is usually a woman (Marge, Lois, Wilma) (per author). Reflective, no data.
why_for_us: Keep one grounded straight character in every scene (Marta or Basia) against Kuba's or Helena's quirks, and leave a beat of silence after each gag, especially with animated/AI characters.

title: ‘Chilled-out entertainers’ – multi-layered sitcom performances in the British and American version of The Office
finding: Performance and textual analysis plus interviews with creative staff: Gervais's and Carell's performances are multi-layered and aimed at different audiences because of the mockumentary discourse, central to each version's embarrassment comedy, and their nuances localise the main character for a domestic audience (per author).
why_for_us: A boss-figure character (Helena) should play two layers at once: what she says to the 'camera' and what her colleagues see; localise her for Polish notarial culture rather than copying US/UK types.

title: Situation Comedy, Character, and Psychoanalysis On the Couch with Lucy, Basil, and Kimmie
finding: Book reading Basil Fawlty, Lucy Ricardo and Kim (Kath & Kim) through psychoanalytic theory to identify elements that must exist in a sitcom 'before the first joke is written', centred on character motivations and the power struggle between characters (per author).
why_for_us: Define each character's want and the office power struggle (senior vs tech-friendly notary, apprentice vs receptionist) before writing gags; the jokes then come from those tensions.

title: Effects of Humorous Disparagement of Self, Friend, and Enemy
finding: Two experiments (72 and 120 undergraduates, audio stories): a self-disparaging humorist was perceived as less intelligent, less confident and less witty than one who disparaged others; females found self-disparagement funnier than males did, while males found disparagement of an enemy funnier (per authors). Old, student samples.
why_for_us: Self-deprecating jokes cost status: give them to Kuba (low status, likeable) rather than to Helena, whose authority the finale depends on.

title: What's so funny? Using a multidisciplinary approach to understand sitcom success
finding: Thesis combining a post-exposure survey of plot and character relatability, a timeline of coded humour events and real-time dial data for Modern Family, The Office, Family Guy and Big Bang Theory; reports new empirical measures predictive of ratings success (per author; abstract gives no effect sizes).
why_for_us: Method model for testing Komputerku pilots: moment-by-moment response (dial or retention curve) plus a relatability survey, mapped against a timeline of each joke.

title: Age differences in the enjoyment of incongruity-resolution and nonsense humor during adulthood.
finding: Survey of 4,292 Germans aged 14-66 rating 20 jokes and cartoons: incongruity-resolution humour increased and nonsense humour decreased in funniness among progressively older participants after the late teens; age differences correlated strongly with conservatism (per authors). Cross-sectional.
why_for_us: Notaries' clients and older viewers will favour jokes that resolve logically (a misunderstanding that makes sense in the end) over absurdist nonsense; keep Kuba's literalism resolvable.

title: Age-related differences in judgments of inappropriate behavior are related to humor style preferences.
finding: Young, middle-aged and older adults discriminated appropriate from inappropriate (gaffe) video clips equally well, but only young and middle-aged adults rated gaffe clips funnier than controls; older adults did not, and young adults' more aggressive humour style mediated the age differences (per authors). Lab experiment.
why_for_us: Cringe/social-gaffe comedy may fall flat with older viewers; if the target audience includes older clients of notaries, base fewer jokes on social embarrassment.

title: The Multiple Meanings of Age for Television Content Preferences
finding: TV ratings data (1970s-1980s) and 2005 survey: age groups differed in genre choices and in the age of characters they watched, and the average age of characters partially mediated age differences in ratings of comedies (per authors).
why_for_us: Viewers gravitate to comedies whose characters are their age; the senior notary Helena is an asset for older viewers and Kuba for younger ones, so give both screen time.

title: Sociality Effects on the Production of Laughter
finding: 162 participants watched a humorous clip alone, with a same-sex stranger or with a same-sex friend: laughter frequency and duration were significantly greater in one or both dyadic conditions than alone, with no differences in self-reported funniness or amusement (per authors).
why_for_us: Phone viewing is mostly solitary, so expect few audible laughs even for good jokes; judge episodes by retention and shares, not by 'laugh-out-loud' reports.

title: Is It Really That Funny? Laughter, Emotional Contagion, and Heuristic Processing During Shared Media Use
finding: Lab experiment (N = 80) with a confederate who laughed or stayed silent: confederate laughter induced participants' laughing/smiling and higher funniness ratings, especially in introverts; low-conscientiousness participants used it as a heuristic cue while high-conscientiousness participants discounted it (per authors).
why_for_us: An on-screen character reacting with amusement (Basia stifling a laugh) can act as an in-story laugh cue without a laugh track, though some viewers will discount it.

title: A mind stretched: The psychology of repeat consumption
finding: Review arguing that repeat consumption (rewatching shows) is less repetitive than assumed: rewatching reveals missed details (stimulus-level novelty) and teaches people about themselves (self-level novelty), so people derive more utility from the familiar than hedonic-adaptation accounts predict (per author).
why_for_us: Hide small background gags (screen text, notes on Helena's desk) that reward a second viewing or a loop of a short clip.

title: Australian medical students' perceptions of professionalism and ethics in medical television programs
finding: Survey of 386 medical students: the most-watched medical programmes were House, Scrubs and Grey's Anatomy; most reported being asked by friends or family about issues shown on programmes, had high recall of ethical topics and believed the programmes generally portrayed professionalism well (per authors).
why_for_us: Professionals do watch comedy about their own occupation (Scrubs was among the top three) and get asked about it, so notaries watching Komputerku will check legal accuracy; keep procedure right even when the joke is absurd.

title: Screen Comedy and Online Audiences
finding: Book studying audience responses posted online to evaluate how viewers judge films and TV shows meant to be funny, and how those criteria relate to social and cultural background and ideas about quality and entertainment (per author). Qualitative analysis of online posts.
why_for_us: Read the comments: viewers publicly argue about what counts as funny; comment threads under episodes are a free qualitative test of which characters and gags work.

title: "Pora umierać"... z takim poczuciem humoru. O śmiechu w filmie i sitcomach
venue: Napis Pismo poświęcone literaturze okolicznościowej i użytkowej
finding: Polish essay asking how a cinema viewer's laughter differs from the amusement of someone watching comedy on a TV screen, combining media studies and psychoanalysis; contrasts cinema's 'voluntary captivity' outside the home with home TV viewing (per author).
why_for_us: Phone viewing is even more private and distracted than home TV; the comedy must work for a solitary, half-attentive viewer, so front-load the hook.

title: Effects of Humorous Heroes and Villains in Violent Action Films
finding: Experiment with an action film edited with and without wisecracks: among female viewers hero wisecracks increased distress during the film but lessened distress at subsequent real violence; males exposed to hero humour found the film marginally less distressing but rated real violence more distressing; villain wisecracks paralleled females' reactions to hero humour (per author).
why_for_us: Jokes inside tense scenes do not simply relieve tension and effects differ by viewer; test any joke placed in a serious client moment (an inheritance dispute) rather than assuming it lightens it.

title: Humor as Camouflage of Televised Violence
finding: Content analysis testing four explanations: the rate of violence (especially verbal) was very high in comedy programmes, mostly minor forms, and the comic context of the portrayals trivialised the violence (per authors).
why_for_us: Comedy trivialises what it frames; jokes about real legal harms (fraud, disinheritance) may read as making light of them, so keep the butt of the joke on the office routine and the AI, not on clients' misfortune.

title: Humorous phenomena in dramatic discourse
finding: Analysis of the medical drama House: conversational humour is prevalent in dramatic discourse (creative metaphor, irony, teasing, non-verbal expression, impersonation), alongside quirky character behaviour, impoliteness, uncanny events, situational irony and deception; these are humorous for the viewer though not necessarily for the characters (per author).
why_for_us: A dry professional (Helena, like House) can be funny to viewers while characters inside the scene take her seriously; her humour can be irony and teasing, not jokes.

title: Horror and Humor
venue: Journal of Aesthetics and Art Criticism
finding: Philosophical essay on horror-comedy: despite seeming opposite mental states (release and lightness vs pressure and claustrophobia), horror and humour are routinely fused, with works shifting moods rapidly 'on a dime'; the essay asks why such fusions can succeed (per author).
why_for_us: Rapid tonal switches are a legitimate tool even in 60-90 s: a tense legal moment can flip into the gag, provided the flip is clean and signalled.

title: Hybridization between the police genre and comedy in American television fiction. ‘Castle’ case study
finding: Case study of Castle: a multidimensional protagonist with a personal backstory lets the police procedural abandon its typical seriousness and rigidity in favour of fun more typical of sitcoms, despite a context of death and crime (per authors). Qualitative, repository version.
why_for_us: Comedy inside a serious professional genre can be carried by one light-hearted lead; Marta (tech-friendly) can be that character against the gravity of notarial deeds.

title: Canned Emotions. Effects of Genre and Audience Reaction on Emotions
finding: Three experiments (N = 110): canned laughter and canned screams had independent effects on amusement and fear and increased immersion when appropriate; enacted (live) sound-tracks had stronger effects; scream tracks worked as well as laugh tracks, especially when the clip was only mildly funny or scary (per authors).
why_for_us: Audio cues shape the genre reading of a scene; a small sound cue (a sigh, a chuckle off-screen) can tell viewers a mildly funny AI-video moment is meant as comedy.

title: The Auditory Kuleshov Effect: Multisensory Integration in Movie Editing
finding: 30 participants watched faces (happy, sad, neutral) intercut with neutral scenes accompanied by happy music, sad music or no music: music significantly influenced emotional judgments of the facial expressions (per authors).
why_for_us: With avatars of limited facial expressiveness, music and sound design can supply the emotion the face cannot; score Helena's deadpan reactions deliberately.

title: How Context Influences Our Perception of Emotional Faces: A Behavioral Study on the Kuleshov Effect
finding: Participants watched film sequences of neutral faces crosscut with happy, fearful or neutral scenes: a significant context effect on valence and arousal appeared in the fear condition only, and participants tended to categorise the neutral face with the context-congruent emotion (per authors).
why_for_us: Context cutting works but not equally for all emotions; do not rely on it alone for comic surprise or amusement, add voice and sound cues.

title: Assessing naturalness and emotional intensity: a perceptual study of animated facial motion
finding: Within-subjects experiment varying auditory emotion level (low/high) and facial motion magnitude (damped/unaltered/exaggerated) of an animated character: auditory expressiveness was positively related to emotion recognition accuracy and perceived intensity; facial motion magnitude raised perceived intensity but lowered perceived naturalness (per authors).
why_for_us: For AI avatars, invest in expressive voices (v3+ TTS emotion tags) rather than exaggerated facial animation, which costs naturalness; the voice carries recognition.

title: Evaluating Animated Characters: Facial Motion Magnitude Influences Personality Perceptions
finding: Two experiments: exaggerated vs damped facial motion changed ratings of cartoon characters' extroversion and competence more than warmth, while for realistic characters it affected extroversion only; in experiment 2 facial motion magnitude influenced respectfulness and calmness but not attentiveness (per authors).
why_for_us: Damped facial motion reads as calmer and can fit the dry senior notary; more motion reads as extroverted, suiting Basia or Kuba; set expressivity per character, not globally.

title: Puppet Animation Films and Gesture Aesthetics
finding: Case studies of three puppet animation films: puppets have limited, wooden-like performance, but these limitations make every nuance important, and gestures are communicated through poses, shots and framings (per authors). Essay.
why_for_us: Limited avatar expressivity can be a style: hold clear poses, frame tightly, and let one small gesture (Helena removing her glasses) carry the beat.

title: Comedians in Cafes Getting Data: Evaluating Timing and Adaptivity in Real-World Robot Comedy Performance
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
finding: Robotic stand-up comedian: in 22 real-world performances a robot with good timing (waiting for audience response) was significantly funnier; in 10 further performances adaptive performance was not necessarily funnier overall, although adaptations almost always improved perception of individual jokes (per authors). Preliminary, small samples.
why_for_us: An artificial performer can be funny if its timing leaves room for response; build in a reaction beat after each line rather than packing AI voice lines back-to-back.

title: TikTok comedy during COVID-19: a multimodal study of platform data, audience engagement, and creative performance
venue: Open Access at Essex (University of Essex)
finding: Thesis (University of Essex), 741 TikTok comedy videos from 14 UK/US creators: likes, comments and shares responded to different multimodal features; role-play (creators embodying distinct characters, 57.4% of the corpus) independently predicted about 21% more likes and 42-48% more shares but not comments (per author). Observational, gender moderated effects.
why_for_us: Character-based role-play sketches are the dominant and best-shared TikTok comedy form; a fixed cast with costumes and relationship stories (the Komputerku approach) matches what gets shared.

title: El humor en TikTok: un caso de estudio de cinco creadores de contenido españoles
finding: Quantitative analysis of 12 months of five Spanish TikTok creators' accounts (n = 914 posts) and content analysis of 70 posts: the most successful humour was affiliative humour about everyday situations, and all technical elements worked to accelerate rhythm (per authors).
why_for_us: Everyday, affiliative office humour (shared frustration with AI credits) fits what performs best in short video; cut fast and avoid dead air beyond the deliberate reaction beat.

title: Taking Humor Seriously on TikTok
finding: Commentary: humour and play are central to TikTok culture through features such as 'Use this Sound' and 'Duet' that invite imitation and transformation; memetic humour serves prosocial aims but viral trends can also trivialise serious harms, so humour should be taken seriously for online safety (per author).
why_for_us: Design a reusable audio hook (the 'feed the little computer' line) that viewers can duet or reuse, while avoiding jokes that trivialise clients' real legal harms.

title: The comedy web series: Reshaping Australian script development and commissioning practices
finding: Analysis of Australian comedy web series (Bondi Hipsters, The Katering Show) and statements by creators and audiences: the web audience acts as a 'comedy gatekeeper' and development is facilitated and influenced by the direct line between creators and viewers (per authors).
why_for_us: Treat early episodes as public development drafts: read viewer comments and adjust characters and gags in later episodes of the season.

title: When Everyone is Laughing: The Presence, Characteristics, and Enjoyment of Disparagement Humor in Online TV
finding: Content analysis: disparagement humour appeared in one in four online TV clips, often targeting appearance and weight, and was often validated by studio audiences, characters and commenters; an experiment found validating audience reaction and existing prejudice predicted enjoyment, and enjoyment predicted willingness to share (per author).
why_for_us: Ridicule spreads online when others validate it; if a character mocks another, the target should be behaviour (Kuba's literalism), never appearance.
